cards.text: The prophet Jeremiah is telling this one himself. After Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carries Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim king of Judah off to Babylon, along with Judah's officials and Jerusalem's craftsmen and metalsmiths, the LORD shows Jeremiah something. It's sitting right in front of the temple of the LORD.

cards.question: What does the LORD show Jeremiah in front of the temple?

answers.text: A branch from an almond tree

cards.text: One basket has very good figs, like those that ripen early. Those are front-row, Display Case, somebody-call-a-PHOTOGRAPHER figs.

cards.question: The figs in the other basket are a little rough, but they're still fine to eat.

cards.text: The LORD asks Jeremiah what he sees, and Jeremiah says, "Figs!" and then gives the full review: the good ones are very good, and the bad ones are very bad, so bad they can't be eaten. Friend, that's me EVERY time an oven door opens: "COOKIES!" and then the full report on which ones came out perfect and which ones came out like hockey pucks.
Then the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah, and plot twist, friend: this was NEVER about fruit. Those two baskets are about people.

cards.question: In the LORD's message to Jeremiah, who are like the good figs?
The LORD says He Himself sent the exiles from Judah away to the land of the Chaldeans.

cards.text: Friend, back in that junk drawer, the only time anybody looked my way was when they were digging for TAPE. These exiles get WAY better: God says He'll keep His eyes on them for good and bring them back to this land.

cards.question: Speaking about the exiles, God says: I will ___ them up and not tear them down; I will ___ them and not uproot them.

cards.text: When I got made new, I got my sharp edges back, and I thought THAT was the best upgrade in history. These exiles get something way better: God says He'll give them a heart to know Him, that He is the LORD.

cards.question: God says the exiles will be His people and He will be their God. What reason does He give?

answers.text: They will return to Him with all their heart
They will build Him a new temple in Babylon
They will win their land back in battle

cards.text: Now the other basket, and friend, I've got the same feeling I get when the timer goes off and I already smell smoke. Like the bad figs, so bad they can't be eaten, that's how God says He'll deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the people of Jerusalem still left in the land.

cards.question: Besides Zedekiah, his officials and the ones still in the land, who else from Jerusalem does God put with the bad figs?
Wherever God banishes the people He compares to bad figs, He says He'll make them a ___ to all the kingdoms of the earth.

cards.text: No jokes on this one, friend. God says He'll send sword and famine and plague against them.

cards.question: God says the sword, famine and plague will keep coming until the people He compares to bad figs have perished from the land He gave them and their fathers.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to pick the exact word 'horror' over 'burden' and 'threat'. No story card sets up verse 9, so nothing the baker has seen lets them reason toward 'horror'. This tests wording they haven't seen, not meaning, so it comes down to luck.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: No story card before this choice card gives any context for verse 9. A thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards can't make a reasoned pick among three negative nouns.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Cards 9 and 11 follow the same template. Each opens with a joke about Papa Dorin's own past (the drawer, then getting renewed), then pivots with 'These exiles get WAY better' and 'These exiles get something way better.' Back to back, it reads like a formula rather than a reaction to the moment.

rule.text: No formula. His personality fits whatever moment he's in, whether it's a tense moment in a story, a hard teaching or a quick question. There are no joke quotas and no required kinds of jokes.

findings.problem: Card 11 ends on God giving the exiles 'a heart to know Him.' The right answer is the only one that repeats 'heart' ('with all their heart'), and it is also the only one in biblical phrasing. That cue makes it stand out from the other two answers.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The question says God 'put[s] with the bad figs' those living in Egypt. Verse 8 is a comparison: 'like the bad figs... so will I deal with.' 'Put with' turns that comparison into a placement. Cards 15 and 17 keep it correctly as 'the people He compares to bad figs.'
